description: I am a major science enthusiast and interested in a multitude of scientific topics having to do with astronomy, astrophysics, and planetary science! My skills include ability to navigate various scientific data sources as well as extract their relavent data to my goals, having a keen understanding of knowledge pertaining to planetary science, and understand physical science of planetary bodies which dictates many chemical and physical make ups of said bodies! Excited to be here!
summary:
I built a route planner for astronauts walking on Mars. You give it real NASA elevation data, and it finds the ground that's too steep or rough to walk on. Then it plans a path from base out to science stops and back that stays off that ground.

The challenge asked for a tool that keeps astronauts safe, so I borrowed rules from Apollo. The big one is that you always have to be able to walk home with oxygen left over. My tool checks that at every single step of the route. It also shows how fast you could get to shelter if a solar storm hit, where you'd lose sight of base, and where long climbs need a rest stop.

I ran it on a real HiRISE map of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. That mattered: my practice terrain looked safe, but real Mars turned up spots the safety checks had to warn about. Planning a walk like this before anyone steps outside could save a life.
details:
What it does and how it works

My project plans a walk for an astronaut on Mars and checks that the walk is safe. It works in four steps. First, a hazard mapper reads a real NASA HiRISE elevation map of north Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, one meter per pixel. For every spot it measures how steep it is, how rough it is, and how much the rocks stick up, then sorts the ground into safe, caution, high-cost, and no-go. Second, a route planner uses A* (a common shortest-path method) to find the easiest path from a base out to two science stops and back, without ever stepping on no-go ground or anything steeper than 22 degrees. It works out walking time step by step, so climbs and rough ground slow you down like they would in real life. Third, a safety layer checks the whole walk against rules Apollo crews used on the Moon. Finally, a map viewer puts it all on one web page you can open offline, with layers you can turn on and off.

On the real terrain the full loop came out to 913 m and about 25 minutes, with zero steps on no-go ground.

Benefits

The big one is that you can catch a problem before anybody steps outside. The safety layer checks every point on the route to make sure the astronaut can always walk home with 30 minutes of reserve left. It also finds the longest it would take to reach shelter if a solar storm hit (6.2 minutes), where the astronaut would lose sight of base (35% of this walk), where long climbs need a rest stop, and how much radiation they'd pick up, using Curiosity's real measurements.

Intended impact

I want this to be a starting point for a real planning tool. A crew or mission planner could load a new piece of Mars, drop in their stops, and get a route with a pass or fail on safety. Next I'd like to add time spent working at each stop, live space weather alerts, and terrain where boxwork has been confirmed.

Tools

Python 3 with NumPy for all the math, and Matplotlib for preview images. The map viewer is HTML5 canvas and JavaScript, packed into one file. No special GIS software, just a laptop. The data came straight from NASA's HiRISE archive in its original PDS format, and I wrote a loader so it only reads the small piece I need out of a 360 MB file.

What makes it creative

Most route planners only ask "what's the shortest path." Mine also asks "if something goes wrong at this exact step, can they still get home?" I took real lessons from Apollo 14, where the crew climbing to Cone Crater couldn't judge distances, ran low on time and oxygen, and turned back about 30 m from the rim, and turned them into checks a computer can run. I also tested on made-up terrain first and then on real Mars. The made-up terrain looked almost perfectly safe. Real Mars didn't, and that difference is the best argument for why you need real data.

Factors I considered

Safety came first, since that's NASA's first priority too. I also thought about how a spacesuit makes walking harder (uphill wears you out, rough ground slows you down), the walkback limits Apollo used, radiation and solar storms, the cold, and keeping line of sight to base for navigation. I was a team of one, so I kept the scope small on purpose: one site, one route, done well. I also wanted to be honest about the limits. My waypoints were chosen for safe ground, not science value, and I didn't confirm boxwork in this patch.

Note: I wrote this page with help from Claude, which drafted the text from my project notes and README. I reviewed and edited it.
